No one will give up the criminalization of the enemy if it proves to be an effective weapon. But in the hands of the West it is not an effective weapon, and cannot be one.
If the West handles its atomic bombs as amateurishly as it handles this weapon—the criminalization of the aggressor—they will be more likely to fall on its own roof than even to touch the real enemy.
I can read Kasack’s The City Beyond the River only as far as Part II, Chapter XIII, p. 290. Then it suddenly turns into caricature and anti-literature. A pity.
The first part very successfully brings Kubin’s The Other Side and Kafka’s The Trial into the world of 1943–44.
Why do all these gifted writers refuse to listen to Ernst Jünger’s warning against every polemical word?

If polemic is no longer directed immediately and completely against a strong enemy who is fully present and has you directly by the throat—as with Léon Bloy or the young Theodor Haecker—but instead against a dead enemy, it immediately begins to squint sideways and is poisoned by the corpse-toxin of the dead enemy.
Later, when I have recovered from the shock of my disappointment, I will continue reading. I hope I will then also be able to judge the appearance of Wilhelm Ahlmann properly.
Léon Bloy’s influence on Ernst Jünger is an extraordinary problem.
Jünger could approach Bloy, the “pariah,” with his savage hatred of Protestants, Prussians, and Germans only by overcoming the strongest possible revulsion.
But Bloy’s diaries are also a prototype for the whole form of the “diary.” I could even say that they helped create the form.

With one stroke they leave behind all that Romantic and impressionistic rummaging through the soul. They make it impossible to confuse “radiations” with “reflections,” and they give the aphorism a concrete situation instead of letting it flutter away into emptiness.
What is magnificent for me—unexpectedly so, beyond anything one could have calculated—is that Ernst Jünger can appear, in this respect, as Léon Bloy’s heir.
Theodor Haecker had long since lost his strong claim to that great inheritance.

But the profiteurs de Léon Bloy—the people who profited from Bloy—such as Claudel, or still more Maritain, threw the inheritance into the street. In return they received the miserable sinner’s wages of satisfying their hatred of a Germany that had already been trampled underfoot.
The baseness of that hatred makes both of them ripe for the curse of today’s pèlerin de l’Absolu—the pilgrim of the Absolute.
To H. Barion, referring to W. Grewe and the discussion of Nuremberg as a legal question:
I ask him to read it,
“so that you will understand why it matters to me that my memorandum on the criminalization of aggressive war was already complete in the summer of 1945, before the indictment was brought.

It stands as a record of the considerations that any lawyer with the necessary expertise could and should already have made at that time—and which one discriminated German lawyer actually did make, without concealing them from anyone, not even from the CIC [Civil Internment Camp].”
For the sake of the German name, and for every lawyer anywhere in the world who thinks scientifically. Also for the honour of the legal profession itself.
Defamed, discriminated against, dismantled, contaminated, underprivileged on every side.
In a dream I say to the Englishman:
Ripe for the final coup de grâce, like Tsar Nicholas of Russia.

Your last move was to accept the unconditional surrender in Schleswig-Holstein, although you had no right to do so. You did not bring about that surrender. The Russians and Americans did. It was not you, but the Russians and Americans, who were masters of both the conflict and what was at stake in it.
The whole argument becomes murky when I think of H. S. Chamberlain.
Wonderful, the Shakespeare passage Günther Krauss copied into his diary Captivitas:
“It is enough for us to know that we are the king’s subjects. If his cause is wrong, our obedience to the king clears us of the crime.”
“Here lies” is the final part of his story. —Daniel Defoe.
Where do those people lie whose ashes an uncomprehending hunger for revenge scattered across the whole world, in the most un-Christian ignorance of the song:
The ashes will not rest, they scatter through every land?
Could they, through the stupidity of their enemies, have escaped the grave?
Defeated in the name of Christianity, we ask ourselves where this Christianity is actually to be found.

I respect the fact that there is a general fear of a contagion de l’infortune—a contagion of misfortune. That respect even gives me a kind of belated satisfaction in my present status, and allows me to draw something useful from my existence as a peripsēma—an outcast, something cast away.
I say satisfaction in my status, because I can no longer claim the honour that once belonged to that status.
On your question about when the idea of “vested rights” was born:
Taken as a whole, the end of vested rights naturally begins when law is transformed into positivist legality.

“Acquired” then simply means légalement acquis—legally acquired—and a single stroke of the legislator’s pen can turn not only whole libraries into wastepaper, but whole paradises of securely acquired rights into piles of rubble.
Modern lawyers have long since begun speaking instead of a situation établie—an established situation—or something similar.
The heart of the problem lies in the relationship between legality and legitimacy.
See my 1932 essay and the question above from 2 March 1948.

Arnold Toynbee (International Affairs, November 1947) attempts the feat of finding a third position, a third force, a third path between capitalist America and communist Russia without becoming fascist. He wants to make Western Europe an independent third factor without allowing Germany to recover its strength.
Europe must not try to become strong again, because Germany might then become strong again.
Better for Europe to perish than for Germany to rise again.
All of this is stated perfectly clearly while remaining peaceful, Erasmian, and never quite spoken outright.
What an immensely cultivated and twisted mind!
In the service of a twisted disposition!

What he calls Western Europe—and from which Germany is excluded—is a bourgeois society in the same social position as the German bourgeoisie in 1919: an intermediate stage between capitalist prosperity and the impoverishment of the underprivileged peoples of Asia.
Germany belongs completely among the underprivileged. So according to Toynbee, Germany has only one option left:
He is the Spengler of the postwar age after the Second World War, just as Churchill became the Clemenceau of the Second World War.
So Claudel has discovered that Germany is the protection and shield of Western Europe against eastern communism (Le Présent, 19 March 1948).
Others had already discovered that when it was not yet too late.
If even Luther in Wittenberg could be called “the soft-living flesh of Wittenberg,” then how should one address Herr von Goethe in Weimar?
Hobbes used to say that it was lawful to use bad instruments for one’s own good.
“If I were thrown into a deep pit,” he said, “and the Devil lowered his cloven hoof down to me, I would grab hold of it and let him pull me out.”
From the biographical introduction to the 1750 edition.
They are all guilty of the same thing. They want to prevent their neighbour from growing stronger.
First France tried to hold down biologically stronger Germany. Then Germany tried to hold down biologically stronger Russia.
Now England, too, wants to hold down Germany and Russia at the same time.
With almost mathematical and physical certainty—and in any case with moral and philosophical-historical certainty—the result will be the liquidation of all of them by Russia.
The most relevant reading today is a history of the age of the Diadochi, the beginning of the Hellenistic period.
For example, Plutarch’s biography of Demetrius Poliorcetes: wild immoralities and violent reversals of fortune, like Adolf’s life—“my life is a novel.”
More interesting than the history of the Caesars, who already sit on top of a fully organized machine of power.
The fantastic theatricality of it all.

The pluralism of these successor-states, no longer capable of unity. Because unity simply for the sake of unity is something for the sort of people Hegel describes when he says: the uneducated person thinks abstractly.
Ernst Jünger says, on the occasion of Arnold Toynbee being brought into the great American defence council, that philosophers of history are now more important than atomic physicists.
As the man who diagnosed the discriminatory concept of war and the transformation of war between states into civil war, I am not surprised.

One becomes even more conscious of Spengler’s genius when comparing him with Toynbee. But Spengler talks too much about Cretans, Hittites, and periods he never experienced himself, but constructed only through parallels, analogies, and similarities.
His universal world history is an imperialist annexation of the past.
Tocqueville is more modest, purer in contemplating his own fate.
Toynbee is both things at once, an English and superior synthesis, but without genuine strength and concerned above all with preventing Germany from rising again.
Perhaps this type of historian has existed only since Versailles in 1919: philosophers of history belonging to decline.

Here a third kind of participant writes history. And Toynbee’s construction of a “third” between West and East—a weak third force whose only purpose is delay—corresponds exactly to this position: the third party sitting between the two sides, the weaker third, the defeated victor.
And for us—and for me personally—very dangerous.
